title: emergencyWithdraw decrements totalStaked without first calling _updatePool, retroactively redistributing the exiting user's in-flight accrual to surviving stakers instead of the protocol
description:
`emergencyWithdraw` mutates `totalStaked` (line 545) and zeros the user's amount/rewardDebt without first calling `_updatePool` to settle accrual since `lastRewardTime`. The function only reabsorbs `pending` computed against the CURRENT (un-advanced) `accRewardPerShare`, which captures only ALREADY-COMMITTED accrual (the portion `_updatePool` had previously moved into `accRewardPerShare`). Any in-flight accrual for the elapsed window `[lastRewardTime, now]` is NOT yet in `accRewardPerShare`, so the exiting user's slice of it is not subtracted. When the next `_updatePool` fires (on a later stake/unstake/claim/admin action), it computes accrual over the FULL elapsed window — which spans both pre- and post-emergency-withdraw periods — at the OLD `rewardRate` but divides by the NEW (smaller) `totalStaked`. The forfeiting staker's intended-to-be-forfeit in-flight accrual is therefore retroactively redistributed pro-rata to the surviving stakers rather than retained by the protocol.

Note: the comment block (L529-537) explicitly acknowledges that 'In-flight accrual since the last `_updatePool` is not yet reflected in `accRewardPerShare`, so it is not subtracted here — it stays in `rewardBudget` and is recycled into the next recompute, which is the correct behaviour.' This is incorrect: leaving it in `rewardBudget` is fine, but the per-share denominator on the NEXT `_updatePool` is the post-mutation `totalStaked`, so the in-flight slice is repriced at a smaller denominator and credited to survivors before the recompute can re-anchor the rate. The 'recycled into rewardBudget' framing only holds if `_updatePool` is called BEFORE the totalStaked mutation.

`_updatePool` itself is internal and side-effect-free with respect to dispatcher liveness (it reads only storage and writes only `lastRewardTime`, `rewardBudget`, `committedDebt`, `accRewardPerShare`); calling it from emergencyWithdraw does not violate the documented escape-hatch property that emergencyWithdraw must work even when dispatcher / NFT minter / recompute path is broken.
impact: Protocol over-emits rewards relative to the advertised `rewardRate * elapsed` for the pre-withdrawal window. Surviving stakers receive a windfall they did not earn under the intended schedule. Forfeited in-flight rewards do not stay with the protocol as the inline comment claims — they are silently redistributed to whoever happens to claim next. With many small emergency withdrawals (e.g. during a migration triggered by `setStakedId`), the cumulative drift can be significant. This also breaks the spec invariant that `accRewardPerShare` advances only at the rate `elapsed * rewardRate / totalStaked` evaluated at the totalStaked in effect during `[lastRewardTime, now]`.
attack_path:
1. Alice and Bob each stake 10 at t=0; totalStaked=20.
2. Bob calls emergencyWithdraw at t=100. totalStaked drops to 10. lastRewardTime is still t=0; accRewardPerShare is unchanged (no _updatePool fired). Bob's `pending` against the un-advanced acc is 0 (rewardDebt was set to amount * acc / 1e18 at stake time and acc has not advanced). Nothing is subtracted from committedDebt or returned to rewardBudget for Bob's [0,100] slice.
3. At t=200 Alice calls claim. _updatePool computes elapsed=200, reward = 200*R, decrements rewardBudget by 200*R, committedDebt += 200*R, accRewardPerShare += 200*R*1e18/10 (NEW totalStaked). Alice's pending = 10 * (200*R*1e18/10) / 1e18 = 200R.
4. Fair allocation: Alice should have earned 50R for [0,100] (pool of 20) plus 100R for [100,200] (pool of 10) = 150R, with 50R retained by the protocol as Bob's forfeit. Actual: Alice receives 200R; the 50R that should have stayed in the pool is silently shifted to Alice.
5. A coordinated griefer can amplify the asymmetry by stacking emergency withdrawals before a claim by another staker, shifting forfeited rewards to whichever surviving staker claims first.
recommendation: Add `_updatePool();` as the first statement in `emergencyWithdraw`, before reading user.amount and computing pending. `_updatePool` short-circuits early when `block.timestamp <= lastRewardTime` and when `totalStaked == 0`, and only touches storage (no external call), preserving the dispatcher-independence guarantee that makes `emergencyWithdraw` an unconditional escape hatch. After the call, re-read `accRewardPerShare` and recompute `pending` so the exiting user forfeits both already-committed AND just-committed slices. Update the inline comment to reflect that in-flight accrual is now settled before mutation.

title: dispatcherHook.mintDebt() trusted as available value in V allows a hostile or buggy hook to over-commit emissions and DoS claims
description:
`_recomputeSchedule` adds `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` directly to V (line 405), which becomes the basis for `rewardBudget = V - committedDebt` and the derived `windowEnd = now + budget/R`. `_syncBudget` measures actual inflow via balance delta around `pull()`, but `_recomputeSchedule` trusts `mintDebt()` as accounting truth. A dispatcher hook that reports `mintDebt` larger than it will actually mint on `pull()` inflates the scheduled runway and lets the contract commit to emissions it cannot pay.

`setDispatcherHook` has no `totalStaked == 0` guard (hook rotation is by design a live operation), no `_syncBudget` / `_recomputeSchedule` call, and no validation that the new hook address actually implements the expected interface. Routes through owner action and is therefore a centralization risk rather than an external-attacker path. The M-01 fix (subtracting `committedDebt` from V) bounds the worst case at runway over-commitment for the un-committed-yet portion, but does not eliminate the surface — `_updatePool` continues to advance `accRewardPerShare` against an inflated `rewardBudget` until the budget runs down, after which `_safePay` reverts with `"NFTStaker: insufficient reward balance"`.
impact: Stakers' accrued rewards become unpayable (frozen behind `_safePay` revert) when the owner installs a hostile or buggy dispatcher hook. Recovery requires owner `topUp` or users taking `emergencyWithdraw` (forfeiting rewards). Principal is always recoverable.
attack_path:
1. Owner (or compromised owner key) installs a dispatcher hook whose `mintDebt()` returns a huge number but whose `pull()` mints little.
2. Any user calls stake/unstake/claim. `_syncBudget` invokes `pull()` (balance delta ~0); `_recomputeSchedule` reads V = balance + hugeMintDebt and extends windowEnd accordingly.
3. Stakers accrue against the inflated `rewardRate * elapsed` window. Eventually `committedDebt > balance` is approached, and `_safePay` starts reverting on every claim.
4. Recovery: owner `topUp`, or users take `emergencyWithdraw` and forfeit rewards.
recommendation: Drop `mintDebt()` from the V computation inside `_recomputeSchedule` (only count actual `balance`), accepting a small lag between pulls — the design already ensures `pull()` runs on every user interaction inside `_syncBudget`, so unpulled `mintDebt` is at most one block's accrual stale. Alternatively, validate that `pull()` actually drained most of `mintDebt` (compare pre/post `mintDebt()` against `inflow`) and revert on shortfall. The current design trusts an external hook for emission scheduling, which is the centralization surface.

title: setDispatcherHook rotation orphans the OLD hook's outstanding mintDebt and leaves rewardBudget stale until corrective action
description: `setDispatcherHook` is the only owner-only setter in this contract that does NOT call `_syncBudget` / `_recomputeSchedule` AND is NOT gated on `totalStaked == 0`. After rotation, `pull()` targets the new hook only — any outstanding `mintDebt` at the old hook becomes unreachable on-chain. The previously computed `rewardBudget` (which included `old_hook.mintDebt()` via the prior `_recomputeSchedule`) is now stale and inflated relative to actual realisable value. The next `_syncBudget` runs `_updatePool` against the stale `rewardRate` and stale `rewardBudget`, advancing `accRewardPerShare` against value the contract cannot redeem, then `pull()` against the NEW hook (which has no debt yet) yields zero inflow, and `_recomputeSchedule` re-anchors V at the new (smaller) balance — but `committedDebt` already absorbed the over-promised slice.
impact: Reward flow can be bricked between rotation and corrective action. Principal is recoverable via `emergencyWithdraw`; rewards are forfeit on that path. Recovery requires owner `topUp` covering the gap or installing a hook with sufficient debt to replace the lost `mintDebt`.
attack_path:
1. Owner rotates `dispatcherHook` while the OLD hook still has outstanding `mintDebt`.
2. Outstanding `mintDebt` becomes unreachable: `pull()` now targets the NEW hook.
3. `rewardBudget` from the prior `_recomputeSchedule` already included the old hook's `mintDebt`. The next user action settles accrual under that stale budget at the stale rate.
4. Subsequent user interactions advance `accRewardPerShare` against the stale budget; eventually `_safePay` starts reverting because actual `balance < pending`.
5. Recovery: owner `topUp` or install a replacement hook with sufficient debt to cover the gap.
recommendation: Either (a) gate `setDispatcherHook` on `totalStaked == 0` to match sibling setters, OR (b) call `_syncBudget()` inside `setDispatcherHook` BEFORE writing the new hook reference (so the old hook's `mintDebt` is realised first via `pull()`), then call `_recomputeSchedule()` after to re-anchor the schedule on the new hook. Sibling setters (`setDispatcherIndex`, `setNFTMinter`) follow option (b)'s shape; this setter is the inconsistent outlier.

title: _recomputeSchedule reads balanceOf(this) directly, allowing donation griefing to extend runway and shift the emission curve
description: `_recomputeSchedule` reads `rewardToken.balanceOf(address(this))` directly into V (line 403), so anyone can transfer phUSD into the staker and have the donation absorbed into `rewardBudget` on the next recompute. No event is emitted for the donation itself (only the indirect `ScheduleRecomputed`). The M-01 fix subtracts `committedDebt` from V, so this no longer over-commits to existing-staker promises, but the surface remains: a donor can unilaterally extend runway and shift `windowEnd` forward outside the operator's intent. The donation cannot be undone by the operator (no withdraw-foreign-tokens function); it accrues to whoever is staked at the time.
impact: Schedule predictability impacted. A donor can anonymously seed the contract before a config change to swing the schedule outside the operator's intent, e.g. front-running a `setTargetAPY` decrease so the lowered rate runs against the donation-inflated budget. No direct fund loss because emissions are still split across stakers proportionally; the operator simply emits more total reward than planned.
attack_path:
1. Owner intends to call `setTargetAPY` to lower the rate — likely because the existing budget is being depleted faster than expected.
2. Attacker (or a friendly LP) front-runs with a phUSD transfer to the staker.
3. Subsequent `setTargetAPY` triggers `_recomputeSchedule` which reads V from the new (donation-inflated) balance, extending `windowEnd` against the donor capital.
4. Operator's emission curve no longer matches their reserved capital; the donor effectively forced the operator to emit at a higher cumulative rate than intended.
recommendation: Track `rewardBudget` as an internal monotonic counter mutated only by `topUp` and the `inflow` delta inside `_syncBudget`. Drop the direct `balanceOf` read inside `_recomputeSchedule`. The recompute should re-derive `rewardRate` and `windowEnd` from the explicitly-tracked budget rather than the live balance. As a side benefit, this also closes the donor-event-silence gap (no mystery balance growth).

title: External NFT mints accelerate runway depletion via latestPrice growth without consent of stakers or operator
description:
`latestPrice = price / r` where `price` is `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex).price` (the NEXT mint price after the most recent mint) and `r = 1 + growthBasisPoints/10_000`. With `growthBasisPoints > 0`, every external mint advances `price` by `price * growthBP / 10000`, growing `latestPrice` geometrically. Because `S = totalStaked * latestPrice` and `R = S * targetAPY / SECONDS_PER_YEAR`, the per-second emission rate scales with `latestPrice`. Anyone able to mint NFTs (which is, by design, any user of the dispatcher) can therefore unilaterally drive up R, accelerating runway depletion against the operator's seeded budget. The spec's APY-as-floor framing accepts this as intentional for reward sizing (early minters earn more than `targetAPY` as a multiple of `r`), but does not address the runway-depletion side effect: an attacker who never stakes, owns no principal at risk, and only mints can force the operator to top up sooner or risk emission cuts.

With `growthBasisPoints == 0` (the spec's collapsed form), `latestPrice = price` is a constant and this surface vanishes. With non-zero growthBP it scales with mint cadence, which is not on-chain bounded.
impact: Runway predictability breaks: operator funds the pool against an expected mint cadence; a hostile minter can drive cadence (and therefore R) far above expectation, draining the budget faster than the seeding curve. Existing stakers receive higher absolute rewards (so the attack does not directly grief them), but the operator must top up more frequently or face premature schedule depletion. Combined with `setTargetAPY`'s same-block reactivity, an operator chasing a runaway latestPrice is forced into reactive policy moves, which themselves require gas and trust. With `growthBasisPoints == 0` this finding does not apply.
attack_path:
1. Operator seeds NFTStaker with budget V intended for a 12-month runway at the expected mint cadence (~10 mints/month) growing `price` from 1e21 to ~1.1e21 over the year.
2. Attacker mints aggressively (e.g. 100 mints in a week) at the dispatcher, pushing `price` to ~2.6e21 a week in.
3. Next user interaction triggers `_recomputeSchedule`, which reads the new price and recomputes R against `latestPrice = 2.6e21/r`. R is ~2.5x the operator's planned rate.
4. `windowEnd = now + budget / R` collapses; runway drops from ~50 weeks to ~20 weeks. Operator must top up or accept depletion.
recommendation: Either (a) document `latestPrice` as a partially-attacker-controlled input and surface a runway-shrink alarm to the operator off-chain, OR (b) cache `latestPrice` at deployment / explicit owner update (e.g. `setLatestPrice(uint256)` gated on `totalStaked == 0`) rather than reading it live from `nftMinter.configs`, accepting that the APY-as-floor framing then requires manual operator updates to track new mints, OR (c) cap `latestPrice` growth between recomputes (e.g. allow at most `r^M` growth per recompute, where M is some operator-set ceiling). Option (a) is lowest-cost and likely sufficient given the centralisation profile of the dispatcher.

title: pendingReward view simulates the next _updatePool but not the next _syncBudget, diverging from claim() output when dispatcher mintDebt has grown since lastRewardTime
description: `pendingReward` simulates the next `_updatePool` step — accruing `elapsed * rewardRate` against the cached `rewardRate` and `rewardBudget` — but does NOT simulate the `_syncBudget` flow that `claim()` actually runs first. `claim` calls `_syncBudget` → `pull()` (which converts pending mintDebt to balance) → `_recomputeSchedule` (which can change `rewardRate` if `latestPrice` or `totalStaked` shifted, though in steady-state it's invariant). Most importantly, between the last on-chain interaction and the view query, `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` may have grown (other contracts pushing debt onto the hook) without `_recomputeSchedule` having absorbed it; `pendingReward` does not re-derive `rewardRate` against the updated V. Front-ends, indexers and auto-compounders that consume `pendingReward` as authoritative claimable receive misleading numbers when the gap between the last interaction and the query is non-trivial.
impact: UX and integrator impact only. Surfaces as front-ends showing a Claim button with a slightly-wrong `claimable` number. No direct asset loss. Minor — typically the divergence is bounded by the time since the last `_syncBudget` and is often zero when interactions are frequent.
attack_path:
1. Last interaction at t=0 caches `rewardRate = R0`. Dispatcher subsequently routes more mintDebt (no on-chain interaction yet).
2. Alice queries `pendingReward` at t=T. View returns `userAmount * (acc + T*R0/totalStaked) / 1e18 - rewardDebt`, computed against R0.
3. Alice calls `claim` at t=T+1. `_syncBudget` pulls the new mintDebt; `_recomputeSchedule` may produce a different R (e.g. if `latestPrice` shifted since t=0) and a different windowEnd; `_updatePool` then uses the cached rate up to the recompute. The view's projection is only correct under the assumption that `rewardRate` has not changed since the last interaction — which is true when only `totalStaked` and `latestPrice` are stable, but the view does not advertise that assumption.
recommendation: Either (a) document `pendingReward` as 'earned at the most-recently-recomputed rate' rather than 'claimable now', and add a sibling view that simulates `_syncBudget` for accurate UI integration, OR (b) refactor `pendingReward` to read live `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` and `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex)` and project a synthetic recompute. Option (a) is simpler and matches existing masterchef conventions.

title: Owner can zero out emissions mid-stake via setTargetAPY(0) or setDispatcherHook(address(0)); no timelock or notice on a user-facing APY commitment
description: `setTargetAPY(0)` is explicitly permitted and immediately drops `rewardRate` to 0 (per CLAUDE.md item 7: 'A == 0 is a supported "pause emissions via APY" mode'). Old accrual is settled at the OLD rate via `_updatePool` before the mutation, but advertised future runway evaporates with no notice or on-chain timelock. `setDispatcherHook(address(0))` similarly removes the `pull()` path and lets the budget drain without further inflows. The `targetAPY` surface is the user-facing commitment of the pool; the absence of any notice window or monotonicity rule means the operator can unilaterally cancel that commitment.
impact: Stakers committed NFTs based on a published `targetAPY` for a published runway. Owner can collapse that runway to zero with no on-chain compensation. Pure centralization. No external-attacker path.
attack_path:
1. Users commit NFTs based on a visible `targetAPY` of 30% with a multi-year runway.
2. Owner calls `setTargetAPY(0)` immediately after a large stake. Runway collapses to zero.
3. Users unstake and receive only the accrual up to the setter timestamp; the advertised future APY is lost.
recommendation: If `targetAPY` is intended as a commitment, add a minimum-notice queue (e.g. APY decreases delayed by 7 days) and/or a monotonicity rule (rate can only fall by at most X% per call). Alternatively, document explicitly in user-facing docs that the APY is mutable at any moment without notice and surface that in the UI.

title: setStakedId mutates the active token ID without recomputing the emission schedule; runway/rewardRate views remain stale until next interaction
description: `setStakedId` is gated on `totalStaked == 0` and writes the new `stakedId`, but unlike its sister setters `setDispatcherIndex` (line 245) and `setNFTMinter` (line 256) it does NOT call `_recomputeSchedule()` after mutation. While `latestPrice` itself is derived from `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex)` (independent of `stakedId`), so `rewardRate` is mathematically unaffected, external views and off-chain indexers driven by `ScheduleRecomputed` events are not notified of the ID change. More importantly: `setStakedId` makes the staker accept a different ERC1155 token ID; existing cached schedule state (computed when the prior stakedId was active) does not signal the operational reconfiguration. This is a state-machine consistency gap rather than an accrual bug.
impact: No principal or reward leak (`totalStaked == 0` short-circuits `_updatePool` and the rate math is independent of stakedId). Inconsistent state surface between sibling admin setters. Front-ends driven by `ScheduleRecomputed` events miss the ID-change boundary and may continue to display schedule data tagged with the prior ID.
attack_path:
1. Owner calls `setStakedId(newId)` when `totalStaked == 0`.
2. No `ScheduleRecomputed` event fires, no `_recomputeSchedule` runs.
3. Off-chain consumers continue to attribute `currentRewardRate` / `runwaySeconds` / `pendingReward` to the prior `stakedId` until a stake / unstake / claim / pullAndRefresh fires.
recommendation: Append `_recomputeSchedule();` to `setStakedId`, mirroring `setDispatcherIndex` and `setNFTMinter`. Alternatively, document explicitly why this setter intentionally leaves the schedule stale. Either path closes the inconsistency without requiring user-facing changes.

title: setPauser accepts address(0), silently disabling the pause/unpause capability
description: `setPauser` performs no input validation. Because the `onlyPauser` modifier compares `msg.sender == pauser`, setting `pauser = address(0)` effectively disables `pause()`/`unpause()` (no `msg.sender` can equal `address(0)` under normal EVM invariants). The global Pauser registration flow expects this contract to be pause-able on demand; an accidental zero assignment silently breaks that emergency invariant. Recoverable by a subsequent owner call but no on-chain guard against the misconfiguration window.
impact: Operational risk: a separately-discovered exploitable vulnerability cannot be mitigated via `pause()` during the window in which `pauser` is mis-set. No external-attacker path.
attack_path:
1. Owner script deploys with an empty env variable resolving to `address(0)` for the pauser.
2. Or owner fat-fingers and calls `setPauser(address(0))`.
3. Pause/unpause is now non-functional; no on-chain alarm.
4. A separately-discovered vulnerability that requires an emergency pause cannot be mitigated until owner re-sets pauser.
recommendation: Add `require(newPauser != address(0), "NFTStaker: zero pauser");` to `setPauser`, OR explicitly document that `address(0)` is a deliberate 'pause disabled' state (and add a separate capability-disable function so the intent is explicit).

title: Admin setters (setDispatcherHook) do not validate that the supplied address conforms to the expected interface
description: `setDispatcherHook` accepts any address (including non-contracts and unrelated contracts) without validating that the target implements `IBalancerPoolerMintDebtHook` (`mintDebt` + `pull`). A misconfigured address causes `_syncBudget` / `_recomputeSchedule` to revert at the external call, blocking stake/unstake/claim. Because `setDispatcherHook` has no `_recompute` and no `totalStaked == 0` gate, a bad hook persists until the next user action reverts; users are then forced through `emergencyWithdraw` (forfeiting rewards) until the owner re-sets the hook. Sibling setter `setNFTMinter` is gated on `totalStaked == 0` AND triggers `_recomputeSchedule` inside the setter, so a bad minter is rejected at setter time (the require self-heals); `setDispatcherHook` is the inconsistent outlier.
impact: Setter misconfiguration freezes the pool for stake/unstake/claim until the owner re-sets the hook; users forced through `emergencyWithdraw` forfeit rewards. Admin-only path. Severity is low because the failure mode is loud (every interaction reverts) rather than silent.
attack_path:
1. Owner scripts a deployment with a bad dispatcher hook address (typo, wrong network, unrelated contract address).
2. Next stake/unstake/claim reverts at `dispatcherHook.pull()` inside `_syncBudget` (or at `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` inside `_recomputeSchedule`).
3. Users either wait for owner to fix or take `emergencyWithdraw` (forfeiting rewards).
recommendation: Probe interface conformance via a low-level `staticcall` to `mintDebt()` in `setDispatcherHook` before persisting (require return data length >= 32, treat as success); optionally also validate `address(newHook).code.length > 0` at setter time. Document this as a liveness probe.
